people.name: Tony Oliva
body: In 2022, more than 45 years after he played his last game, Tony Oliva was inducted into the National Baseball Hall of Fame. He had spent his whole major-league career with the Minnesota Twins, from 1962 to 1976.

Oliva was born on July 20, 1938, in Pinar del Río, a farming province in western Cuba. He signed with the Twins in 1961 and played that season for their minor-league club in Wytheville, Virginia, reaching the majors in September 1962, in the years when the break in U.S.–Cuba relations was cutting Cuban players off from home.

His start was remarkable. In 1964 he won the American League batting title and was named AL Rookie of the Year. He won the title again in 1965, which made him the first player to win batting crowns in his first two full seasons, and he won a third in 1971. His career ended with 1,917 hits, 220 home runs and a .304 batting average. Knee injuries shortened his playing days.

In his final season, 1976, he was also a Twins coach. He stayed in Minnesota and stayed with the team, as hitting coach for the 1987 World Series champions and bench coach for the 1991 champions. MLB.com reports that he is the only person to have been part of all three Twins pennant winners (1965, 1987 and 1991). He later became an analyst on the Twins' Spanish-language radio broadcasts and a special assistant in the front office.

In December 2014, when the United States announced it would restore diplomatic relations with Cuba, MPR News asked Oliva for his reaction. "I've been waiting for that for 50 years," he said. "I think it's beautiful."
keyFacts: 1938: Born July 20 in Pinar del Río, Cuba.
1962–1976: Played his whole major-league career with the Minnesota Twins.
1964: AL Rookie of the Year and batting champion; batting titles again in 1965 and 1971.
Career totals: 1,917 hits, 220 home runs, .304 average.
1987 and 1991: Twins hitting coach, then bench coach, on World Series champions.
2022: Inducted into the National Baseball Hall of Fame.
people.connectToWork: When someone's family is divided by a border or by politics, how would that change the way you ask about relatives, emergency contacts or who can help?

people.name: Zoilo Versalles
body: In 1965 the Minnesota Twins reached their first World Series, and their leader in the field was a 25-year-old shortstop from Havana. That year Zoilo Versalles won the American League Most Valuable Player award. According to the Society for American Baseball Research (SABR), he was the first Latin American-born player, and the first player born outside the U.S., to win a major-league MVP award.

Versalles was born on December 18, 1939, in the Marianao section of Havana, to a family of modest means. He came into the majors with the Washington Senators. When that franchise moved to the Twin Cities in 1961 and became the Twins, he moved with it. He played shortstop for the Twins through 1967 and won Gold Glove awards in 1963 and 1965.

After he was traded to the Los Angeles Dodgers in November 1967, his career declined. He played for several teams, in the Mexican League, and in Japan in 1972. He came back to the Minneapolis area, where the years after baseball were hard. He had chronic back problems, two heart attacks and long periods without work. He lost his house to foreclosure and sold his MVP trophy, Gold Gloves and All-Star rings.

He was found dead in his rented home in Bloomington on June 11, 1995, and coroner’s tests showed he had apparently died two days earlier, on June 9. The Twins inducted him into the team Hall of Fame in 2006.
keyFacts: 1939: Born December 18 in Marianao, Havana, Cuba.
1961–1967: Played for the Minnesota Twins after the Senators moved.
1963 and 1965: Won Gold Gloves.
1965: AL MVP, the first Latin American-born MVP by SABR's account.
1995: Died June 9 in Bloomington, Minnesota.
2006: Inducted into the Twins Hall of Fame.
people.connectToWork: When someone was once widely celebrated and now needs help, how would you make sure your questions about money, health and work do not assume what they already know or have?

people.name: Camilo Pascual
body: In 1961, the Minnesota Twins' first season, the team's best pitcher was a Havana-born right-hander known for one of the best curveballs of his time. Camilo Pascual led the American League in strikeouts in each of his first three seasons in Minnesota, from 1961 to 1963.

Pascual was born in Havana on January 20, 1934. He reached the majors with the Washington Senators in 1954. At that time the Senators were known for signing Cuban players, and a network of Cuban scouts and players helped bring young men from the island to the U.S. He moved to Minnesota with the franchise and pitched for the Twins from 1961 to 1966. Baseball-Reference credits him with seven All-Star selections over his career, counting each game in the years when two were played.

When his playing days were over, Pascual spent decades as an international scout. SABR reports that he scouted for the Oakland Athletics from 1982 to 1988, signing José Canseco for Oakland, and joined the Los Angeles Dodgers in 1989, covering Venezuela. The Twins inducted him into their Hall of Fame in 2012. He entered an exile-run Cuban hall of fame in Miami in 1983, and in 2014 he was among the first ten people named to the re-established Cuban Baseball Hall of Fame in Havana.
keyFacts: 1934: Born January 20 in Havana, Cuba.
1954: Debuted with the Washington Senators.
1961–1966: Pitched for the Minnesota Twins; led the AL in strikeouts 1961–1963.
1982–1988: Scout for Oakland; joined the Dodgers in 1989.
2012: Inducted into the Twins Hall of Fame; 2014: named to the Cuban Baseball Hall of Fame in Havana.

people.name: Marisella Veiga
body: On December 30, 1960, four-year-old Marisella Veiga boarded a plane from Havana to Miami with her mother and two brothers. Her father followed a few months later. He had arrived in the U.S. with 14 cents, and he moved the family to Minnesota for better job prospects, where he became an assistant comptroller at a meat distributing company in St. Paul. A host family helped them settle.

Decades later she wrote about that move in a memoir, We Carry Our Homes With Us: A Cuban American Memoir, published by the Minnesota Historical Society Press on April 15, 2016. It describes her family's adjustment to the Upper Midwest in the 1960s and 1970s, along with their Cuban friends. She has said she wants it to give voice to immigrants and show what assimilation involves.

Raised in St. Paul and Miami, Veiga became a writer, poet and journalist. When the book appeared in 2016, NBC News described her as a writer and professor in northern Florida, and the publisher's page for the book lists her as an adjunct instructor at Flagler College, living in St. Augustine. Her book is a first-person account of one Cuban family's life in Minnesota, published by the state's own historical press.
keyFacts: 1960: Left Havana for Miami at age four, on December 30; the family later settled in the Twin Cities.
Her father worked for a St. Paul meat distributing company.
2016: We Carry Our Homes With Us published by the Minnesota Historical Society Press on April 15.
Publisher's page for the 2016 book: writer and adjunct instructor at Flagler College, St. Augustine, Florida.
people.connectToWork: If someone is one of very few people from their background in your town, what would you need to do differently when you connect them with services or other people?

people.name: Celia Cruz
body: In 1960 Celia Cruz left Havana with her band, La Sonora Matancera, on what was billed as a tour. She never went back. The Cuban government refused to let her return, including when she asked to visit her sick mother, who died in 1962. In exile she became the "Queen of Salsa" and one of the most famous Afro-Latina performers in the world.

Cruz was born in Havana on October 21. Her official site and the National Women's History Museum give the year as 1925; the National Park Service and Brooklyn College give about 1924. She was an Afro-Cuban singer whose music came out of the African-rooted traditions of Cuban popular music, and in 1950 she became the lead singer of La Sonora Matancera.

In the early 1960s she married trumpeter Pedro Knight. In the 1970s she became a central figure in New York's salsa scene, recording for Fania's Vaya label from 1974, starting with the album Celia & Johnny with Johnny Pacheco. She was famous for her cry of "¡Azúcar!" ("Sugar!") and her bold wigs. In 1994 she received the National Medal of Arts.

She died on July 16, 2003, at her home in Fort Lee, New Jersey. Her dress, wig and stage shoes went to the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History, which opened an exhibit about her, "¡Azúcar!", in 2005.
keyFacts: Born October 21, 1924 or 1925, in Havana; sources differ on the year.
1950: Became lead singer of La Sonora Matancera.
1960: Left Cuba and never returned.
1974: Began recording for the Vaya label.
1994: Awarded the National Medal of Arts.
2003: Died July 16 in Fort Lee, New Jersey.
people.connectToWork: If someone has not been able to go home for a parent's illness or death, how would you leave room for that in a conversation about family and support?

people.name: Minnie Miñoso
body: When Minnie Miñoso stepped onto the field for the Chicago White Sox in 1951, he was a Black Cuban player in a sport that had only just begun to integrate. He became one of the most exciting players of the 1950s.

Miñoso was born on November 29, 1923, in Perico, Cuba, though SABR notes that his family later gave 1925. The major leagues were segregated until 1947. Miñoso first played in the Negro Leagues, for the New York Cubans from 1946 to 1948, and helped the team beat the Cleveland Buckeyes in the 1947 Negro League World Series.

When he debuted with Cleveland on April 19, 1949, he became, in the Hall of Fame's words, the first acknowledged dark-skinned Latin player in AL/NL history. Cleveland traded him to the White Sox on April 30, 1951. When he debuted for Chicago the next day, he homered and became the first Black player on the White Sox.

The Hall of Fame counts nine All-Star Games. Chicago became his home, and he died there on March 1, 2015. In December 2021 the Golden Days Era Committee elected him to the Baseball Hall of Fame, and he was inducted in 2022 in the same class as Tony Oliva.
keyFacts: 1923: Born November 29 in Perico, Cuba.
1946–1948: Played for the New York Cubans (Negro Leagues).
1951: Debuted with the Chicago White Sox on May 1, the team's first Black player.
Named to nine All-Star Games, by the Hall of Fame's count.
2015: Died March 1 in Chicago.
2022: Inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame.
people.connectToWork: Your forms may ask about race and ethnicity separately. How would you make sure a person who is both Black and Cuban can say so in their own words?

people.name: Ileana Ros-Lehtinen
body: In 1989 Ileana Ros-Lehtinen won a special election in Miami for the congressional seat left open by the death of Representative Claude Pepper. According to the House's official history, she was the first Hispanic woman and the first Cuban American elected to Congress.

Ros-Lehtinen was born in Havana on July 15, 1952, and left Cuba with her family at age eight, shortly after Fidel Castro came to power. She grew up in Miami, and the House history describes her as a prominent critic of Fidel Castro's communist government. With her parents she co-founded Eastern Academy, a private elementary school, where she was a teacher and chief administrator. She served in the Florida House from 1982 to 1986 and in the Florida Senate from 1986 to 1989.
She served in the U.S. House from 1989 until January 2019. From 2011 to 2013 she chaired the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the first woman to lead it.
keyFacts: 1952: Born July 15 in Havana, Cuba.
About 1960: Left Cuba with her family at age eight.
1982–1989: Florida House, then Florida Senate.
1989: Won a special election; the first Cuban American in Congress.
2011–2013: Chaired the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the first woman to do so.
1989–2019: Served in the U.S. House.

people.name: Oscar Hijuelos
body: In 1990 a novel about two Cuban brothers, musicians playing mambo in 1950s New York, won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction. Its author, Oscar Hijuelos, became the first Latino writer to win the prize. The Mambo Kings Play Songs of Love had been published in 1989, and it was later made into a movie starring Armand Assante and Antonio Banderas.

Hijuelos was born in New York City in 1951 into a family that had come to the United States from Cuba, and he grew up there, well before the large migration that followed 1959. He wrote eight works of fiction and a memoir, Thoughts Without Cigarettes (2011), about his family's arrival from Cuba.
From 2008 until his death he taught in Duke University's English department. He died suddenly in Manhattan on October 12, 2013, at age 62, of a heart attack while playing tennis.
keyFacts: 1951: Born in New York City to a family from Cuba.
1989: The Mambo Kings Play Songs of Love published.
1990: Pulitzer Prize for Fiction, the first Latino winner.
2008–2013: Taught English at Duke University.
2011: Memoir, Thoughts Without Cigarettes.
2013: Died October 12 in Manhattan, at 62.

people.name: Evelio Grillo
body: Growing up in Ybor City, Tampa's Cuban cigar-making neighborhood, Evelio Grillo learned early that the Cuban community was split by race. In an oral history he said, "Black Cubans were closer to black Americans and white Cubans were closer to white Americans." Under Jim Crow, he went to segregated Black schools.

Grillo was born in Tampa in June 1919 to Cuban parents. He went to Dunbar High School in Washington, D.C., a well-known all-Black school, and to Xavier University in New Orleans. In World War II he served in the segregated 823rd Engineer Aviation Battalion in the China-Burma-India theater, where he helped build the Ledo Road and put out a daily newspaper, The Hairy Ears Herald. He left the Army as a staff sergeant.

After the war he earned a master's degree in social welfare at UC Berkeley in 1953. In Oakland he directed the Alexander Community Center, worked as a community relations consultant, and was the first Black employee in the city manager's office. He volunteered with the NAACP and the Mexican-American Political Association. From 1977 to 1979 he was an executive assistant for policy development at the U.S. Department of Health, Education and Welfare under President Carter.

His memoir, Black Cuban, Black American (Arte Público Press, 2000), is an account of Afro-Latino life in the U.S. Radio Bilingüe says he dedicated the last years of his life to building bridges between African Americans and Latinos in Oakland.
keyFacts: 1919: Born in Tampa (Ybor City) to Cuban parents.
World War II: 823rd Engineer Aviation Battalion, a segregated unit, China-Burma-India theater.
1953: Master of Social Welfare, UC Berkeley.
1977–1979: Worked at the Department of Health, Education and Welfare under President Carter.
2000: Published Black Cuban, Black American.
people.connectToWork: Which of your partners are organized by language and which by race? Who might not feel at home in either, and how would you find out?

people.name: Carmen Herrera
body: Carmen Herrera painted for decades with almost no sales. She sold her first painting in 2004, at age 89. Twelve years later, in 2016, the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York gave her a solo exhibition, Carmen Herrera: Lines of Sight. Her bold, hard-edged geometric paintings are in the collections of the Whitney, the Museum of Modern Art and Tate Modern in London.

Herrera was born in Havana on May 30, 1915. Her father was the founding editor of the Havana newspaper El Mundo, and her mother was a reporter. She studied architecture at the University of Havana in 1938–1939. There she met an American teacher, Jesse Loewenthal. They married and moved to New York in 1939.

From 1948 to 1953 the couple lived in Paris, where Herrera turned toward geometric abstraction and showed her work five times at the Salon des Réalités Nouvelles. She settled back in New York in 1954 and kept painting in the same Lower Manhattan loft for about 60 years. El Museo del Barrio said she had been passed over in favor of European and U.S. male artists, and her later gallery, Lisson, wrote that being a Latina woman may have slowed her early career. She died at home in Manhattan on February 12, 2022, at age 106.
keyFacts: 1915: Born May 30 in Havana, Cuba.
1939: Married Jesse Loewenthal and moved to New York.
1948–1953: Lived in Paris; settled in New York in 1954.
2004: Sold her first painting, at age 89.
2016–2017: Carmen Herrera: Lines of Sight, Whitney Museum of American Art.
2022: Died February 12 in Manhattan, at 106.
people.connectToWork: Whose work does your organization only notice late, or after someone else has recognized it? What would you change in how you look?

people.name: Mirta Ojito
body: In 1980 a teenage Mirta Ojito left Cuba with her family aboard a boat called Mañana, one of the thousands of vessels in the Mariel boatlift. The boat belonged to a Vietnam veteran, and it carried the family across the Florida Strait to a new life in Miami. Years later she would retrace that crossing in a memoir.

Ojito was born in Havana about 1964 and was about sixteen when the family left. Her parents opposed the Communist government and had waited about twenty years for a chance to leave, so when Castro opened the port of Mariel the family moved quickly. As a girl she had wanted to join the Young Pioneers, but she grew disillusioned as she came to understand the repressive side of the revolution.

In the United States she earned a degree from Florida Atlantic University and a master's degree from Columbia University. She reported for the Miami Herald and El Nuevo Herald before joining The New York Times, where she contributed to the series "How Race Is Lived in America," which won the 2001 Pulitzer Prize for national reporting. She also received the American Society of Newspaper Editors' award for best foreign reporting. Her memoir, Finding Mañana: A Memoir of a Cuban Exodus, tells her own story and seeks out the people who set the exodus in motion. She has taught journalism at Columbia University, New York University and the University of Miami.
keyFacts: Born in Havana about 1964.
1980: Left Cuba at about sixteen in the Mariel boatlift, on the boat Mañana.
Reported for the Miami Herald, El Nuevo Herald and The New York Times.
2001: Contributed to the Times series that won the Pulitzer Prize for national reporting.
Author of Finding Mañana (paperback 2006).
Has taught journalism at Columbia, NYU and the University of Miami.
people.connectToWork: When you hear that someone is Cuban, how would you learn when and how they came, rather than assuming which departure, which years and which memories are theirs?

people.name: Cristina Saralegui
body: In 1989 Univision launched a new Spanish-language talk show from Miami, hosted by a magazine editor. El Show de Cristina ran for 21 years and made Cristina Saralegui one of the best-known faces in Spanish-language media in the United States.

Saralegui was born in Havana on January 29, 1948, by the Hollywood Walk of Fame's account (Brooklyn College gives 1949). After the Cuban Revolution, her family fled to Miami in 1960. She studied journalism and communications at the University of Miami. In 1973 she began an internship at the magazine Vanidades, and in 1979 she became editor of the Spanish-language edition of Cosmopolitan, based in Miami, leading it for more than a decade.

On November 4, 1999, she received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. Her show last aired on November 1, 2010. She also wrote the memoir Cristina!: My Life as a Blonde (1998). By 2007 she had won 12 Emmy Awards, and in 2005 GLAAD gave her its Valor Award for educating viewers about gay and lesbian issues and AIDS awareness.
keyFacts: 1948: Born January 29 in Havana.
1960: Family moved to Miami.
1979: Became editor of the Spanish-language Cosmopolitan.
1989: Launched El Show de Cristina on Univision.
1998: Memoir, Cristina!: My Life as a Blonde.
1999: Star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.
2005: GLAAD Valor Award; 12 Emmys by 2007.
2010: Show's final broadcast on November 1.

people.name: José Martí
body: On January 31, 1895, José Martí left New York City for the last time. He had lived there for most of fifteen years, writing, organizing and raising money among Cuban exiles. Now he was going home to fight in the war for Cuban independence from Spain. On May 19, 1895, he was shot and killed by Spanish troops at Dos Ríos, in eastern Cuba. He was 42.

Martí was born in Havana on January 28, 1853, when Cuba was a Spanish colony. As a teenager he was arrested in 1869 for criticizing Spanish rule and sentenced to hard labor. He was released in 1871 and deported to Spain, where he studied law. He later lived in Mexico and Guatemala.

Around 1880 he settled in New York, after a brief stay in Venezuela. He made his living as a journalist, writing for New York publications such as The Hour and The Sun and for La Nación of Buenos Aires, explaining the United States to readers across Latin America. He also served for a time as consul in New York for Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay. In the second half of 1891 he began resigning his posts as foreign correspondent and diplomat to devote himself to Cuban independence.

In 1892 he helped found the Cuban Revolutionary Party, built on support from Cuban exile communities. On March 14 of that year he launched its newspaper, Patria, the voice of Cuban and Puerto Rican emigrants in the United States. His work in New York shows that the Cuban independence movement was organized in large part on U.S. soil, by an immigrant community.
keyFacts: 1853: Born January 28 in Havana.
1869: Arrested for opposing Spanish rule; deported to Spain in 1871.
About 1880–1895: Lived mostly in New York as a writer and organizer.
Wrote for La Nación (Buenos Aires); served as consul for Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay.
1892: Helped found the Cuban Revolutionary Party and its newspaper, Patria.
1895: Killed May 19 at Dos Ríos, Cuba.

people.name: Desi Arnaz
body: On October 15, 1951, I Love Lucy premiered on American television. Its co-star, playing bandleader Ricky Ricardo, was a Cuban immigrant with a strong accent who did not hide it. Desi Arnaz was also, behind the camera, one of the most important business minds in early television.

Arnaz was born on March 2, 1917, in Santiago de Cuba, into a wealthy family. During the Cuban revolution of 1933, the family home in Santiago was ransacked and burned. His father, a newly elected congressman, was jailed, and the family fled to Miami. The teenager went from privilege to odd jobs, including cleaning birdcages for a canary dealer.

Music opened the door. He played guitar with the Siboney Septet, worked briefly for bandleader Xavier Cugat in New York, and then led his own band. He is credited with introducing the conga line to American audiences. While starring in the film Too Many Girls, he met Lucille Ball. They married in 1940.

The couple founded Desilu Productions in 1950 and kept full ownership of I Love Lucy. Arnaz is credited with creating the three-camera, live-audience method that became standard for sitcoms. In 1955 the show began rebroadcasting earlier episodes, the first reruns of a current prime-time show. The Television Academy says he sold his half interest in Desilu to Ball in 1962; PBS gives 1963. He died of cancer at his home in Del Mar, California, on December 2, 1986.
keyFacts: 1917: Born March 2 in Santiago de Cuba.
1933: Family fled to Miami after the Cuban revolution of 1933.
1940: Married Lucille Ball.
1950: Co-founded Desilu Productions.
1951: I Love Lucy premiered October 15.
1986: Died December 2 in Del Mar, California.
people.connectToWork: When a person's accent or English is different from what your process expects, what do you assume about their skill or authority? What would you check first?

people.name: Roberto C. Goizueta
body: When Roberto Goizueta left Cuba for Miami around 1960, he had to restart his life in a new country. Two decades later he was running the Coca-Cola Company.

Goizueta was born in Havana on November 18, 1931. He studied at the Belén Jesuit school in Havana, spent a year at Cheshire Academy in Connecticut, and earned a bachelor's degree in chemical engineering from Yale University in 1953. In 1954 he answered a help-wanted ad and took a chemist's job with Coca-Cola's Havana subsidiary.

After Fidel Castro came to power, Goizueta left for Miami; sources give 1960 or 1961. His family lived for a time in a motel room. He kept working for the company as an engineer for its Latin American operations, and after Miami he was posted to Nassau, in the Bahamas. In 1964 he moved to headquarters in Atlanta. He became a vice president in 1979, president and chief operating officer by 1980, and chairman and chief executive in 1981. Diet Coke was introduced in 1982. During his roughly sixteen years at the top, the company's stock value rose by more than 7,000 percent.

He died of lung cancer in Atlanta on October 18, 1997, at age 65. His name is on the University of Miami's Roberto C. Goizueta Pavilion, which houses the Cuban Heritage Collection, profiled on this page.

1953: B.S. in chemical engineering, Yale University.
1954: Joined Coca-Cola's operation in Cuba.

1981: Became chairman and CEO of the Coca-Cola Company.
1997: Died October 18 in Atlanta.

people.name: Catarina Rivera
body: Catarina Rivera is a deafblind Latina of Cuban and Puerto Rican heritage. She grew up in Maryland with Spanish as her first language and began wearing hearing aids as a toddler. At 17 she was diagnosed with Usher syndrome, which affects hearing and vision. She uses a white cane.

She taught as a bilingual elementary school teacher with Teach for America, earned a master's degree in public health, and worked for New York City nonprofits on food justice and community engagement. In 2020 she started the Instagram account @blindishlatina. She now works as a public speaker and consultant on disability, has given a TEDx talk, creates accessible travel content, and founded Blindish Latina LLC.
Writing in Remezcla, she calls herself a disabled Latina woman and says "I'm deafblind due to Usher syndrome."
keyFacts: Heritage: Cuban and Puerto Rican.
Grew up in Maryland; Spanish was her first language.
Diagnosed with Usher syndrome at 17; describes herself as deafblind.
Master of Public Health.
Founder of Blindish Latina LLC; TEDx speaker and disability consultant.

people.name: Gloria Estefan
body: In March 1990, singer Gloria Estefan's tour bus was caught in a seven-mile pileup during a snowstorm in Pennsylvania's Pocono Mountains. The crash fractured her back and compressed her spinal cord. Surgeons fused her vertebrae with steel rods, screws and hooks. She spent a month in the hospital and about six months in daily rehabilitation before she felt she could perform again.

Estefan was born in Havana on September 1, 1957. In 1996 she became chair of the capital campaign for the Miami Project to Cure Paralysis, which raised money for the Lois Pope LIFE Center at the University of Miami, opened in 2000. BrainHealth puts the total at about $47 million. The Miami Project says she has been part of its family for decades, and she has served as Mistress of Ceremonies at its Great Sports Legends Dinner.

We found no statement that she calls herself disabled, so this page does not use that word for her. Her public work on this subject has centered on research toward a cure, which is one view among disabled people and not a shared one.
keyFacts: 1957: Born September 1 in Havana.
1990: Tour bus crash; spinal cord compression and back fracture; spinal fusion.
From 1996: Chaired the Miami Project's capital campaign.
2000: Lois Pope LIFE Center opened.
2015: Received the Presidential Medal of Freedom with her husband, Emilio Estefan.
people.connectToWork: When someone with a new injury tells you what they hope for, how would you support that hope and also make sure they hear about the supports available now?

institutions.name: Cuban Heritage Collection, University of Miami
body: In the late 1960s, a group of Cuban exile librarians at the University of Miami began documenting exile life, tracking arrivals on the Freedom Flights that were announced on Spanish-language radio. Their goal was to save materials that could one day be taken back to Cuba. The university later backed their work: in 1980 the library set up a Cuban Collection with Esperanza Bravo de Varona as its archivist, and in 1995 supporters formed the Amigos group. In 1998 the University of Miami formally established the Cuban Heritage Collection.

The university honors five women as its founders: Rosa M. Abella, Ana Rosa Núñez, Esperanza Bravo de Varona, Lesbia Orta Varona and Gladys Gómez-Rossié, all librarians there. Most of the collection is housed in the Roberto C. Goizueta Pavilion of the Otto G. Richter Library.

The university describes it as the largest repository of Cuban documents outside the island. Holdings include more than 200,000 documents, a signed first edition of José Martí's Ismaelillo, a rare letter from independence hero Antonio Maceo, Celia Cruz's flag and shoes, and the Lydia Cabrera Collection. Its Luis J. Botifoll Oral History Project has recorded more than 100 interviews with Cuban American leaders, and its fellowship program has supported more than 80 doctoral researchers.
keyFacts: Late 1960s: Exile librarians began documenting exile life.
1980: The library set up a Cuban Collection.
1998: Formally established as the Cuban Heritage Collection.
More than 200,000 documents.
Luis J. Botifoll Oral History Project: more than 100 interviews.
institutions.connectToWork: If people lost their records when they left a country, what does your process do when it asks for documents they cannot produce?

institutions.name: American Museum of the Cuban Diaspora
body: For about ten years a banner reading "Cuban museum coming soon" hung on a building at 1200 Coral Way in Miami. On November 19, 2016, the museum behind it opened its doors; Miami Today later called that a soft opening and reported a grand opening planned for September 8, 2018. Its founding director, Ileana Fuentes, called it a "museum of memories," a place where exiles could reconnect with their past.

The museum was founded in 1996 as the "Cuban Museum" by Dr. Ofelia Tabares and a group of Cuban American community leaders, and for years it worked without a permanent home. Fuentes said the old name "could mean anything about Cuba." It was renamed the American Museum of the Cuban Diaspora, known as The Cuban, to make clear that its subject is the Cubans who left the island and the art they made abroad. Its opening show featured the exile artist Luis Cruz Azaceta.

As of October 2026 it is open daily, with a permanent exhibit on Cuban exile history, live theater and rotating exhibits. It also runs political projects, including "The Cuban Deck" with the Foundation for Human Rights in Cuba and a petition on a United Nations vote about Cuba, so it speaks from one position among the views Cuban Americans hold.
keyFacts: 1996: Founded as the "Cuban Museum."
2016: Opened at 1200 Coral Way, Miami, on November 19.
Founded by Dr. Ofelia Tabares and community leaders; founding director Ileana Fuentes.
First featured artist: Luis Cruz Azaceta.
institutions.connectToWork: When an institution tells a group's story, whose memories does it hold, and who else would you need to hear from before you rely on it?

institutions.name: Institute for Cuban Studies, Florida International University
body: In 1991 Florida International University, in Miami, created a center devoted to "creating and disseminating knowledge about Cuba and its diaspora." Its founding director was the sociologist Lisandro Pérez, who led it for twelve years. Long known as the Cuban Research Institute, it had taken the name Institute for Cuban Studies by 2026.

The institute runs conferences, lectures, book presentations, film screenings and concerts. It offers scholarships and research travel grants, and it lists Hemisphere Magazine and the FIU Cuba Poll, a survey of Cuban American opinion, among its work. It belongs to the Inter-University Program for Latino Research. Its funders have included the Ford, MacArthur, Mellon and Rockefeller foundations, the National Endowment for the Humanities and the National Science Foundation.
keyFacts: 1991: Founded at Florida International University.
Founding director: Lisandro Pérez.
By 2026: Renamed from Cuban Research Institute to Institute for Cuban Studies.
Lists the FIU Cuba Poll and Hemisphere Magazine among its work.

institutions.name: Parent to Parent of Miami
body: Parent to Parent of Miami is a Miami-Dade nonprofit that supports families of children and adults with disabilities. It runs a federally funded Community Parent Resource Center for families of people from birth to age 26 with any disability, and it offers parent-peer support on early intervention, education, employment and disability law, with workshops and coaching.

Its Spanish-language side, Padre a Padre de Miami, describes free information, education and emotional support, from staff who are trained parents, family members and special education professionals. It serves Miami-Dade, which has a large Cuban American population, but it is not a Cuban organization and does not publish what share of its families are Cuban. We found no Cuban-specific disability organization in Minnesota.

IRS ruling year: 1990.
Community Parent Resource Center, birth to age 26.

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Here, Cuban means people who trace their family to Cuba, whether they came in the years after 1959, in the 1980 Mariel boatlift, in the 1990s, after 2000, or were born in the U.S. They differ by generation, race, faith, politics and income. We did not find a Minnesota study, or any peer-reviewed study centered on how Cuban American families understand disability. What follows rests on one Miami study of people caring for older adults and one policy brief about Cuba itself, and research on Cuba is not research on Cuban Americans.
questions: When did you or your family come to the U.S., and what were disability services like where you lived before?
How do you and your family talk about what's going on? What words do you use for it?
Who gave you a diagnosis or a label? Has it helped?
What do you want a label or assessment to open up for you? Is there anything you want it to avoid?
Who helps with care and decisions now? Who do you want involved, and who not?
Which language do you want to use, and does it matter to you what kind of Spanish your interpreter speaks?
What would make outside help acceptable to you, such as help at home, a break for the person giving care, or Spanish-speaking staff?
Do you have questions about who sees the information you give us?
Is faith or a spiritual practice part of how you deal with this? Is there anyone from it you would like us to include?
What words do you want us to use for your disability, if any?

context.heading: What one Miami study found about family care
body: Friedemann and colleagues (2013) interviewed 595 people caring for frail older adults in the Miami-Dade area, 185 of them Cuban. They were caring for older adults, not children with disabilities. About 61 percent were randomly selected through five home health agencies and the rest came through neighborhood leaders, and the authors call the design correlational with many small ethnic effects.

Among the four groups compared, Cuban caregivers reported the greatest family stability, the longest caregiving hours and the lowest sense of burden. Their sense of obligation was the highest, though not significantly different from the others. The authors suggest that many were older spouses who had immigrated and come through hardship together. That is a finding about one sample, not a description of any family.

sources.label: Friedemann, Buckwalter, Newman and Mauro, Journal of Cross-Cultural Gerontology (2013)

context.heading: Low service use is not low need
body: In the same study, Cuban caregivers used the fewest community services of the four groups, a mean of 1.12 in the past month against 1.55 for white caregivers. The authors link this to patterns among foreign-born Hispanic people more widely. It may reflect a family's capacity, barriers, or both. Do not read it as a lack of need, or as refusal. Check hours, cost, language and agency rules before reading it as culture.

We could not establish from Cuban-specific sources whether distrust of government systems, immigration status or cost act as barriers. Explain plainly who sees a person's information. If immigration status comes up, explain what eligibility rules require and refer to legal aid instead of guessing.

sources.label: Friedemann, Buckwalter, Newman and Mauro, Journal of Cross-Cultural Gerontology (2013)

context.heading: What a brief about Cuba itself says
body: A 2008 policy brief on intellectual disability in Cuba (Brice) reports that families traditionally provide care, that false beliefs about causes and social stigma persist, and that intellectual disability is understood mainly as a social problem. Special schools were created by ministerial resolution, adult rehabilitation includes "defectology," and approaches for adults include segregated and institutional elements. The author also says family involvement in special education and rehabilitation remains limited.

This is one author, writing about Cuba in 2008. It can help you ask what someone who arrived recently expects, including separate schools or settings. Whether any of it carries over among Cuban Americans has not been well studied.

sources.label: Brice, Journal of Policy and Practice in Intellectual Disabilities (2008), abstract

context.heading: Faith and healing
body: In the Miami study, Cuban caregivers scored 3.98 on a spirituality scale, between white (3.67) and other Hispanic (4.34) caregivers, and the authors concluded that spirituality was comparable across groups. That study gives no reason to expect faith to matter more or less for a Cuban family.

Faith may be Catholic, Protestant, Jewish, an Afro-Cuban religion such as Santería, Espiritismo, or none. We found published work on Santería and Espiritismo in health among Cuban Americans but could not read it, so this page makes no claim about it. Ask openly, without judging, and involve a religious leader or practitioner only if the person wants that.

sources.label: Friedemann, Buckwalter, Newman and Mauro, Journal of Cross-Cultural Gerontology (2013)

context.heading: Words and language
body: Terms used in Cuba's system include defectología ("defectology") and escuelas especiales (special schools). In U.S. practice the first carries a deficit meaning, so avoid it. Use the person's own words: Catarina Rivera, profiled on this page, calls herself a disabled Latina woman and deafblind. We found no source on Cuban-specific terms that carry stigma, and none on gender roles or who makes decisions, so ask each person.

Do not assume any Spanish interpreter will suit, or that Spanish is wanted at all. By Minnesota Compass's account, more than three-quarters of Cuban Minnesotans were born in the U.S. Offer plain-language written materials in English and Spanish.

context.heading: Who is missing
body: We found no Minnesota disability organization specific to Cuban people, and no national Cuban American one. The community routes below are not Cuban-specific. Parent to Parent of Miami, profiled on this page, shows one model of parent-peer support in English and Spanish. Do not treat any one person or organization as speaking for everyone.

communityRoutes.name: CLUES Abriendo Caminos Behavioral Health Clinic
communityRoutes.purpose: Behavioral health services from Minnesota's largest Latino-led nonprofit, at 2600 East 25th Street, Minneapolis. It is not Cuban-specific. CLUES also has locations in St. Paul, Willmar and Austin.

organizations.intro: Minnesota's Cuban community is small, and we found no Cuban American association, club, church ministry or business group here. The Latino agencies and Spanish-language media below are general starting points; we found no source on which ones Cuban Minnesotans use. A few cultural groups and restaurants are the visible Cuban-focused places. Minnesota Compass lists 8,775 Cuban Minnesotans in American Community Survey data for 2020–2024 (give or take 1,811), a sample estimate (the Census Bureau’s Hispanic-origin count for the same years is lower, 6,536, give or take 994), and says more than three-quarters were born in the U.S., without a year for that figure. MPR News reported about 3,600 in 2014, about 1,000 of them born in Cuba; the two numbers use different years and methods, so they do not measure growth. Nationally, Pew estimates 2.4 million people of Cuban origin in 2021, about 53 percent born abroad. The list is a set of starting points for learning, it is not complete, and Cuban Americans hold a wide range of political views that no one group here speaks for.

entries.name: Comunidades Latinas Unidas En Servicio
entries.location: St. Paul, Minneapolis, Willmar and Austin
entries.purpose: Founded in 1981, and describes itself as Minnesota's largest Latino-led nonprofit. Programs include behavioral health, career training, elder programs, children and parenting, and community resources. Serves all Latino people, not Cuban people specifically.

entries.name: Cuban American Youth Orchestra
entries.purpose: Grew out of the Minnesota Orchestra's 2015 tour to Cuba. Runs music exchanges for students between Minnesota and Cuba and, now, across Latin America. It received Minnesota Arts and Cultural Heritage funding, most recently found for fiscal 2023.

entries.name: Minnesota Cuba Committee
entries.purpose: Says it is committed to the sovereignty of the Republic of Cuba, and supports ending the U.S. embargo and travel ban. Helps run the yearly Minnesota Cuban Film Festival. It holds one position on U.S.–Cuba policy, and Cuban Minnesotans hold many.
entries.linkLabel: KSTP interview with the committee about its film festival

entries.name: Minnesota Cuban Film Festival
entries.purpose: Running since 2010, with a 17th edition reported in spring 2026. It is coordinated by the Minnesota Cuba Committee with the Film Society of Minneapolis St. Paul and Cuba's national film institute.
entries.linkLabel: Prensa Latina, Cuban state news agency, on the 2026 festival

entries.name: Victor's 1959 Cafe
entries.purpose: A Cuban restaurant. Minnesota Monthly (May 2015) says it was opened by Victor Valens, a native of Cuba, after he found no other Cuban restaurants in the Twin Cities. It is a business, not a community organization.

entries.name: El Cubano
entries.purpose: Serves Cuban and Dominican food. We could not establish whether its owners are Cuban. It is a business, not a community organization.

entries.name: Guavas Cuban Cafe
entries.purpose: Opened about 2018 in the Diamond Lake area and serves Cuban breakfast and lunch. We could not establish whether its owners are Cuban. It is a business, not a community organization.

entries.name: Our Lady of Guadalupe Church
entries.purpose: The first Spanish-speaking Catholic church in Minnesota, with Spanish Masses on Sundays. We found no Cuban group named at this parish, so it is a general Spanish-language contact.

entries.name: Church of the Incarnation
entries.purpose: A south Minneapolis Catholic parish with a Sunday Mass in Spanish, also known as Sagrado Corazón de Jesús. We found no Cuban group named at this parish, so it is a general Spanish-language contact.

entries.name: La Prensa de Minnesota
entries.purpose: Started in St. Paul in 1991 by Mario Duarte. MNopedia calls it the state's first statewide Spanish-language and bilingual paper. It has been published inside Vida y Sabor, and its site carries local, national and world news.

entries.name: El Rey 94.9 FM
entries.location: West St. Paul, 149 Thompson Avenue East
entries.purpose: Spanish-language music, entertainment, news and educational programs. Not specific to Cuban listeners.

entries.name: El Minnesota de Hoy
entries.purpose: A daily Spanish-language news and information site for Latino people in Minnesota, with health, immigration, politics and entertainment.

entries.name: Cuban American National Foundation
entries.purpose: A long-standing Cuban exile group, founded in 1981. Its stated mission is to empower Cuban civil society to build a durable democracy in Cuba. It filed a federal Form 990 for fiscal 2024. Its website currently shows little beyond its name and social media links.

entries.name: Cuban American Bar Association
entries.purpose: A bar association of judges, lawyers and law students. It works on diversity in the judiciary, funds scholarships and runs a pro bono project for people with low incomes. It also works with the opposition coalition Acuerdo de Liberación on a legal transition in Cuba. It has no Minnesota presence.

entries.name: Catholic Charities of the Archdiocese of Miami, Refugee Services
entries.type: Faith-based human services and refugee resettlement
entries.purpose: Resettlement and job services, including Cuban/Haitian Services that help people reach community resources. CBS Miami reported in April 2026 that a federal contract for its care of unaccompanied migrant children was being ended, so check what is still running.
